explanations.explanation: Horses, baker! Isaiah says they "rely on horses," and then he keeps going with "their abundance of chariots" and "their multitude of horsemen" (Isaiah 31:1). That's a whole stable, a parking lot of chariots and a cheering section. Everything they're leaning on has hooves or wheels, and none of it is the LORD.

Ships sound fancy, but Isaiah never mentions a single one. He says they "rely on horses" and trust in chariots and horsemen (Isaiah 31:1). Nobody is checking the harbor in this verse. Everything on that list stays on dry land and has hooves or wheels.

Walls are a solid guess, but Isaiah doesn't list any here. What he says is that they "rely on horses," with chariots and horsemen right behind them (Isaiah 31:1). Their trust is in things that gallop, not things that stand still. It's a whole lot of motion for people who need a place to be safe.

I see why you'd think it, but it's the opposite. Isaiah says of them, "They do not look to the Holy One of Israel; they do not seek the LORD" (Isaiah 31:1). They're staring at the horses and not at Him. Nobody can look two directions at once, not even me with a mustache.

False, and Isaiah says it plainly: "They do not look to the Holy One of Israel; they do not seek the LORD" (Isaiah 31:1). Their eyes are on the horses, the chariots and the horsemen. The LORD isn't even on the list, and that's exactly why the woe comes.

explanations.answer: He does not call them back
explanations.explanation: Yes! Isaiah says of the LORD, "He does not call back His words" (Isaiah 31:2). Once He's spoken, it stands. No take-backs, no "let me rephrase that." I wish I had that kind of follow-through. I once said "just one more cookie" about forty times.

Not quite. Isaiah says the opposite: "He does not call back His words" (Isaiah 31:2). When the LORD speaks, He doesn't go back and swap it out. His word stays put, and that includes the part about disaster.
Close, but no. Isaiah doesn't say anything about hiding. He says, "He does not call back His words" (Isaiah 31:2). The words have been spoken, out loud, and they aren't getting pulled back.

That's it! Isaiah says He "will rise up against the house of the wicked and against the allies of evildoers" (Isaiah 31:2). Notice that the helpers are in there too, not only the folks being helped. Think about that next time you're about to sign on with a crowd.

Good guess, but Isaiah doesn't name kings here. He says the LORD "will rise up against the house of the wicked and against the allies of evildoers" (Isaiah 31:2). The second group is the allies, the ones who team up with evildoers.

That's a name from other stories, but it's not in this verse. Isaiah says the LORD "will rise up against the house of the wicked and against the allies of evildoers" (Isaiah 31:2). The second group he names is the allies, the helpers who back up evildoers.

Both, baker. Isaiah says "the helper will stumble, and the one he helps will fall; both will perish together" (Isaiah 31:3). The helper doesn't get to watch from the sidelines and neither does the one leaning on him. It's like two people holding each other up on a wobbly ladder when the ground goes.

Not just the helper. Isaiah says the helper will stumble and the one he helps will fall, and then adds, "both will perish together" (Isaiah 31:3). The one being helped doesn't walk away. They go down side by side.

Not only that one. Isaiah says "the helper will stumble, and the one he helps will fall; both will perish together" (Isaiah 31:3). The helper doesn't get a pass. Both of them are in the same boat, and the boat is going down.

True! The LORD says the lion "is not terrified by their shouting or subdued by their clamor" (Isaiah 31:4). A whole band of shepherds is yelling, and that lion just keeps standing over its prey. I'd have been halfway to the next county. My mustache would've been a white flag.

Other way around. The lion "is not terrified by their shouting or subdued by their clamor" (Isaiah 31:4). The shepherds are called out against it and they make plenty of noise. It doesn't move an inch.

Do battle, yes! The LORD says, "so the LORD of Hosts will come down to do battle on Mount Zion and its heights" (Isaiah 31:4). He's the one coming down, and the lion picture is how He says it. Nobody's shouting Him off the mountain.

Nice thought, but that's not in this verse. The LORD says, "the LORD of Hosts will come down to do battle on Mount Zion and its heights" (Isaiah 31:4). The lion picture is about a fight, not a construction project. Hard hats stay in the truck.

Tempting if you like tidy numbers, but no. The LORD says He "will come down to do battle on Mount Zion and its heights" (Isaiah 31:4). A lion standing over its prey isn't taking attendance. It's a battle picture.

Protect! "Like birds hovering overhead, so the LORD of Hosts will protect Jerusalem" (Isaiah 31:5). Birds hover over what they're watching over, and that's the picture here. Good, warm words after all that woe.
I get it, after all that woe it might feel that way. But the verse says the LORD of Hosts "will protect Jerusalem" (Isaiah 31:5). Birds hovering overhead stay right there. They don't leave.

Not this time. The verse says, "Like birds hovering overhead, so the LORD of Hosts will protect Jerusalem" (Isaiah 31:5). There's no test in this picture. Hovering birds are staying close, and that points to protecting.

Return to Him, baker! The message says, "Return to the One against whom you have so blatantly rebelled, O children of Israel" (Isaiah 31:6). The way back is open, and it's a way home. I know a little about being found, so I like this one a lot.

No hiding in this message. It says, "Return to the One against whom you have so blatantly rebelled, O children of Israel" (Isaiah 31:6). The call is to turn around and come back, not to duck behind a bush.

Not gifts. The message says, "Return to the One against whom you have so blatantly rebelled, O children of Israel" (Isaiah 31:6). It's the coming back that matters here. Nobody's asked to show up carrying a fruit basket.

Idols! The message says, "every one of you will reject the idols of silver and gold that your own hands have sinfully made" (Isaiah 31:7). Their own hands made them, and then they bowed to them. I make cookies with my stamper, but I have never once asked a cookie for advice.

Altars is a reasonable guess, but that's not the word here. The message says, "every one of you will reject the idols of silver and gold that your own hands have sinfully made" (Isaiah 31:7). The word is idols, and their own hands made them.

Silver and gold do sound like crown material. But the verse says, "every one of you will reject the idols of silver and gold that your own hands have sinfully made" (Isaiah 31:7). They're idols, not crowns, and they were made by the hands that now turn from them.
Right! The LORD says, "a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals" (Isaiah 31:8). Assyria falls "not by the sword of man." No blacksmith signed that blade, and no army carries it.

Egypt is the wrong place to look, since that's where the trouble started. The LORD says, "a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals" (Isaiah 31:8). It's not forged by anyone, in Egypt or anywhere else.

Good thinking, but the LORD says it's not that kind of sword. Assyria will fall "not by the sword of man; a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals" (Isaiah 31:8). No human army holds it, Judah's included.
Not this time. The LORD says "They will flee before the sword" (Isaiah 31:8). Assyria doesn't dig in and fight it out. They run, and that's the opposite of standing their ground.

False, baker. The LORD says, "They will flee before the sword, and their young men will be put to forced labor" (Isaiah 31:8). Nobody stands and fights. They run for it, and I think I'd be right there running with them.

explanations.answer: The sight of the battle standard
explanations.explanation: Yes! "Their princes will panic at the sight of the battle standard," declares the LORD (Isaiah 31:9). No swinging, no shouting, just a banner showing up. I'd panic too if the oven timer went off and I hadn't started the dough.

Tambourines make it sound like a party. But the verse says "their princes will panic at the sight of the battle standard" (Isaiah 31:9). It's something they see, not something they hear, and it's a battle banner.

Egypt's chariots were part of the first trouble, but they aren't named here. The LORD declares, "their princes will panic at the sight of the battle standard" (Isaiah 31:9). That banner is what sets the princes off.
